opus-5.5.text:
I think the way I'd frame it is: which uncertainties actually change the decision someone would make? There are a lot of ways a benchmark number can be off, and many of them are interesting but don't matter much for the questions we care about, which are roughly "could this model do something dangerous?" and "how fast is this going?"

So the first big bucket I worry about is elicitation. If we under-elicit a model, because we gave it a bad scaffold, too little inference compute, or didn't fix some silly tool-use issue, we can underestimate what it can actually do by a lot. And that error is asymmetric. Overestimating capabilities is embarrassing, but underestimating them is the failure mode that actually matters for safety. People downstream, whether that's a lab, a fine-tuner, or a motivated bad actor, will put much more effort into getting performance out of a model than we can in a few weeks of evaluation. So a lot of our attention goes to asking how much headroom there is that we're not seeing.

The second bucket is how well the tasks represent the real world. Benchmark tasks tend to be well-specified, self-contained, and automatically scorable, and real work is messy. There are implicit requirements, you have to gather context, and "done" isn't clearly defined. So there's a real question of whether, when we say a model can do tasks that take a human two hours, that transfers to two-hour tasks in an actual codebase or an actual research project. We've seen evidence that the gap can be substantial, so I think that one deserves a lot of scrutiny, especially when people extrapolate trends.

Then there's the more statistical stuff: noise from small task sets, how you estimate human baseline times, the choice of success threshold. I take these seriously, but they're often more tractable. You can put error bars on them, rerun with different assumptions, and see whether the qualitative conclusion holds. If the trend line's slope is robust to reasonable choices there, I worry less.

The heuristic I come back to is to look for the uncertainties that are both large and systematic, ones that could push every result in the same direction, rather than ones that just add noise. Elicitation gaps and task representativeness are systematic in that way. They don't average out when you add more tasks. So that's where I'd spend the effort.

r001.rationale: The response says real-world task transfer can be a substantial gap and that statistical errors can be handled with error bars, but it does not state that generalization uncertainty usually greatly exceeds standard-error-based error bars.

r002.rationale: It explicitly prioritizes uncertainties by whether they change decisions about the underlying questions, such as whether a model could do something dangerous or how quickly capabilities are advancing.

r003.rationale: It names threat and progress questions and discusses task representativeness, but does not propose deriving the benchmark properties from those questions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing is to ask what question the benchmark is actually supposed to answer, and most of the time the question we care about isn't "what score does the model get," it's something like "how close is this to being able to do dangerous or economically important work autonomously?" Once you frame it that way, a lot of the sources of uncertainty people fixate on turn out to not matter very much, and some that get ignored matter enormously.

The ones I tend to prioritize are the ones that could flip the conclusion rather than just move the number a bit. So, for instance, the amount of elicitation effort. If you run a model with a bad scaffold and no tool access and it gets ten percent, and then someone spends two weeks on prompting and agent infrastructure and it gets fifty percent, that's not noise, that's a completely different picture of the world. And it's systematically biased in one direction: you can always have under-elicited, you basically never over-elicit. So we spend a lot of effort trying to establish that we're not leaving large capability on the table, and when we can't rule that out, I'd rather say so loudly than report a clean-looking number.

The second thing is task validity, meaning does success on the task actually mean what we're claiming. Contamination is the obvious version, but there's a subtler one, which is that a task can be solvable in some degenerate way that doesn't require the skill you were trying to measure. We've had cases where a model gets a task right, you look at the transcript, and it's guessed the answer or exploited something about the grading. If you don't read transcripts, you don't catch that, and the uncertainty is invisible to statistics.

Then there's the question of what the human baseline actually is. A lot of the time people compare against a human number that was collected under totally different conditions, different time limits, different incentives, different expertise. That comparison is doing a lot of work in the headline claim, so if it's shaky, the whole claim is shaky.

What I'd put lower on the list, honestly, is run-to-run sampling variance. People love confidence intervals because they're easy to compute, but with a reasonable number of tasks and runs it's often a smaller effect than any of the things I just mentioned, and reporting tight error bars can create a false sense of precision when the real uncertainty is in these structural things.

So the heuristic is roughly: which sources are large, which are directionally biased rather than symmetric, and which would actually change what a decision-maker should do. Elicitation and validity hit all three. And then the honest thing is to report the result alongside those caveats in a way that makes it hard to strip them off and quote just the number.

r001.rationale: It says run-to-run sampling variance is often smaller than structural uncertainties such as elicitation and task validity, but does not clearly state that uncertainty about real-world generalization usually greatly exceeds standard-error error bars.

r002.rationale: It prioritizes uncertainty sources that could change the conclusion or what a decision-maker should do, starting from the question the benchmark is meant to answer.

r003.rationale: It frames the benchmark’s purpose in terms of dangerous or economically important work, but does not clearly propose deriving the benchmark’s needed properties from questions about AI threats or real-world impacts.

astra-6.text:
I think the main question is: could resolving this uncertainty change the decision we make? You can spend a lot of effort getting a very precise score on a benchmark, but if you’re unsure whether that benchmark measures the capability you actually care about, that precision may not help very much.

So I’d start with the claim we’re trying to support. Are we asking whether a model can do a task under a particular setup, or whether someone could get it to do that task with more effort? Those are different questions. A failure might reflect a limitation of the model, but it might also reflect the prompt, the tools, or how much opportunity it had to try different approaches.

I’d prioritize uncertainties that could substantially change our interpretation, especially where we have some practical way to investigate them. For example, does performance improve a lot with better scaffolding? Are the tasks representative of the real work? Can we reliably tell whether an attempt succeeded? The aim is to identify the uncertainty that matters most for the conclusion, rather than just the one that’s easiest to put an error bar on.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether a precise benchmark score measures the capability of interest, but does not say that real-world generalization uncertainty usually exceeds standard-error error bars.

r002.rationale: It recommends prioritizing uncertainties that could substantially change the interpretation or decision and that matter most to the conclusion.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes benchmark questions about task performance under different setups and asks whether tasks represent real work, but does not propose deriving benchmark requirements from questions about AI threats or real-world impacts.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by asking which uncertainties could actually change the decision we’re trying to make. If we’re using an evaluation to decide whether a model can carry out some dangerous task, then uncertainty about whether our test elicits its capabilities matters a lot. A low score could mean the model can’t do it, or it could mean we used a poor prompt, gave it the wrong tools, or didn’t allow enough attempts. Those have very different implications.

I’d also distinguish uncertainty about performance on the benchmark from uncertainty about what that performance tells us about the world. You can measure a benchmark score quite precisely and still have a very uncertain answer to the question you actually care about.

So I’d prioritize uncertainties that are both consequential and tractable: where plausible answers would lead us to take different actions, and where doing another experiment could meaningfully distinguish between them. I wouldn’t necessarily spend the most effort on whichever uncertainty is easiest to put an error bar around.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes precise benchmark scores from uncertainty about what they imply, but does not say that real-world generalization uncertainty usually greatly exceeds standard-error error bars.

r002.rationale: It prioritizes uncertainties by whether they could change the decision or meaningfully affect the answer to the question of interest.

r003.rationale: It gives a dangerous-task evaluation as an example, but does not propose deriving benchmark properties from the intended threat or real-world impact questions.
